implementation_notes: TypeORM maps the dependent with an ordinary one-to-many whose cascade covers insert/update and whose orphanedRowAction: 'delete' removes rows that dropped out of the parent's collection when the parent is saved; saving the parent therefore persists the child set, and the child repository should not be exposed. Relations must be loaded on the instance before saving, because TypeORM only cascades what the entity actually references. It is framework configuration rather than a hand-written mapper, but the contract is the pattern's: the parent's persistence path owns the children.
pitfalls: orphanedRowAction only fires for saves that load the relation: a partially populated Order persists what is attached and can delete the rest.
cascade: true also propagates remove to whatever object happens to be attached, and TypeORM only traverses loaded relations.
The child still needs its @ManyToOne foreign-key column; without onDelete: 'CASCADE' the database has no backstop for a parent delete.

variants.name: Prisma nested writes
variants.idiom_name: nested create / deleteMany + create on the parent relation
variants.implementation_notes: Prisma has no change tracking, so the dependent mapping is expressed as nested writes from the parent: create writes parent and children in one call, and an update with a nested deleteMany plus create replaces the child set, with Prisma supplying the foreign key itself; there is no child repository beyond the generated client, and the child is only reachable through its parent relation. The classic delete-and-reinsert is written by the developer, but it stays a single parent-owned operation.
pitfalls: A nested deleteMany + create rewrites every child row, so child-side ids change and anything referencing them breaks.
Nested writes are only atomic inside one call - splitting the delete and the create across two client calls loses the parent's transaction, use $transaction if you must.
